title: Why he never learned to read and his melodic drum style
summary: He declined studio reading work, and describes his accented triplets and melodic approach versus modern drummers.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah. The creative part was missing. That's why I didn't want to learn how to read music and learn how to play legitimate drums and then do all that. I could have probably worked in studios out there in California and said, uh, Big Boynton wanted me to play drums. He said, I'll show how to read all this stuff. I said, Vic, I don't want to do all that. I said, I want to play my jazz my way and make people happy my way.
Because I'm not the best, I said, but it sure is different than the rest.
Mm-hmm. So that's the way things work out with me. It's a little different than all these guys playing today. These guys playing today, they got all this bunch of drums, and they go, all eight notes.
You see, when I play eight notes, I play, but the accent, the triplet, and it makes it walk a little better. You know what I mean? And it's a little different style than a monotone sound.
And I think you get more sounds out of a drum kit than other drummers. That's it.

I play a melody. A lot of guys say he plays a melody drum. Mm-hmm. I mean, that's the way I always, like, just like a trumpet player would play a chorus. I'm singing a chorus all the time in my head, but I wouldn't want to play on a trumpet.
You know, or lead the chorus, whatever we do, you know. So that's what I've been doing, playing it that way. I've always played that way.
